title: Website handover checklist: domains, source code, analytics and access
AI title: Website handover checklist: domains, source code, analytics and access
excerpt: Verify domain, code, hosting, analytics and enquiry access with practical tests before accepting a website handover.
imageAlt: Gold icons for domain, code, analytics and access in a digital handover case.
content:
A website handover is complete when your team can renew the domain, update the site, deploy a change, receive enquiries and recover from a mistake without relying on one person's login. A folder of files is useful, but it does not prove any of those things. Ask for an inventory of the accounts and assets, agree who controls each one, then test the everyday tasks with your own accounts before the handover closes.

This checklist is for businesses taking over a new site or moving from one agency to another. It works for a small brochure site as well as a site with a content system, external forms and multiple integrations. The goal is not to remove the agency from every account. It is to make continued support a choice rather than a dependency.

## Start with an inventory you can maintain

Make one row for each service or asset. Include its name, provider, account or project identifier, business owner, technical contact, billing owner, renewal timing and the action still outstanding. A useful status is “invitation accepted, deployment not yet tested,” not simply “done.” Keep passwords, backup codes and private keys out of the inventory. If a secret must change hands, use your approved secure process rather than a project spreadsheet.

Distinguish three things: who controls the account, who pays for it and who can carry out routine work. A finance employee might receive hosting invoices without being able to deploy. An agency might have permission to publish without owning the hosting account. Those arrangements can be perfectly workable, provided everyone knows who can grant access, change payment details or recover the account when a person leaves.

List the systems even if they look incidental. A forms provider, image library, search index, translation service or email relay can be essential to the public site. The quickest way to find omissions is to walk through a real customer visit and name the systems involved at each step. Then repeat that exercise with a content editor and someone responsible for paying the bills.

## Domain, DNS and email

Record the domain registrar, the business contact responsible for renewal, the account recovery method and the DNS provider. These may not be the same company. Ask who can change nameservers and who manages the active DNS records. Review the current DNS configuration and keep a secure reference copy so the next person is not trying to reconstruct it from memory.

Moving the site to another host does not necessarily mean transferring the registration. A registrar move, a change to the listed registrant and a change to DNS are different operations. [ICANN’s registrant transfer guidance](https://www.icann.org/resources/pages/name-holder-faqs-2017-10-10-en) explains these distinctions and identifies circumstances that can delay some transfers. Check the rules for your particular domain and provider before using a transfer date as a launch commitment.

Check email separately from the website. Confirm which records support incoming mail, sending authentication and any third-party verification. If the project changes DNS, test incoming and outgoing business mail as well as the public website. A homepage that loads does not tell you that purchase enquiries still reach the sales team. Have the people who normally send and receive that mail confirm the result before closing the change.

## Source code, design files and content

Ask for the canonical repository, not only a compressed copy of the latest files. Record the production branch, the approval process for changes and which commit corresponds to the current release. Confirm whether the site is built from one repository or several. Include instructions for obtaining dependencies, building the project and locating the publishable output. Note anything that runs separately, such as a backend or a recurring import.

The business needs the access appropriate to its agreement. If a GitHub transfer is part of the plan, read [GitHub’s repository transfer documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/transferring-a-repository) before moving it and inspect the resulting settings afterward. A repository move is not a substitute for reconnecting a deployment service or checking who can approve a change. Verify private repository access from the receiving account and check that the host pulls from the intended location.

List design source files, approved artwork, content exports and licensed assets separately. A PDF preview is not an editable design file. A set of static HTML files is not a database export. For third-party fonts, stock images or paid plugins, record who holds the licence and what must be renewed or replaced. Ask for the original files your agreement includes, without assuming that every template or asset can be transferred under the same terms.

Include a short note on how published content maps to editable content. Show where the team edits a service page, how to add an image with a suitable alternative description, and how to unpublish a time-sensitive announcement. If only a developer can make a common change, record that dependency plainly rather than presenting the site as fully self-service.

## Hosting, deployment and recovery

Record which hosting project serves production, which environment is used for previews and how a change moves between them. Ask the current operator to show a small deployment from start to finish. An authorised member of the receiving team should repeat the process in a preview environment, check the change and identify the last known good release. That is more valuable than a recording of someone else clicking Publish.

A working environment needs more than source code. Record required configuration names and where their values are managed, without pasting secret values into documentation. Include custom build settings, scheduled jobs and service connections. After changing an integration credential through an approved process, verify the feature before retiring the old credential. Coordinate changes with the people who own the connected system.

Ask what recovery means for your particular site. Restoring a previous front-end build may not restore content, orders or uploaded files. Identify what is backed up, how often and who is authorised to request or perform a restoration. Test recovery in a safe environment with suitable data rather than restoring over a production site just to see whether it works. Record what the test did and did not cover.

## Analytics, tracking and search visibility

Start by finding the property that actually receives the production site's traffic. Note its name and identifier, who controls it and which reports the business relies on. If the site uses a separate tag-management container, record that as another account with its own access and publishing responsibilities. Check which measurement tags and conversion events are intended to run. More tags are not proof of more useful reporting.

Use the [Google Analytics access management guide](https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9305587?hl=en) to distinguish account-level from property-level access and match roles to responsibilities. An analyst who can read reports does not necessarily need authority to change configuration. Conversely, if no one at the business can manage access where required, having a report open on their screen does not solve the ownership problem.

Verify Search Console independently. Check that the business controls the relevant property and understands its verification method. [Google’s Search Console permissions documentation](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7687615?hl=en) distinguishes verified owners from delegated ones and explains why old verification tokens matter. Establish and test the business's ownership first. Before removing an old token, identify where it lives and confirm what else depends on it.

Run a controlled test for an agreed business action, such as submitting a labelled test enquiry. Confirm the website response, the destination inbox or system, and the intended measurement event using the team's normal diagnostic method. If a transaction completes on another platform, document what the website can measure and what only that provider reports. A click on a booking button should not be recorded as a confirmed appointment unless the implementation can verify the difference.

## Prove the enquiry handoff still works

Write down the destination for each important path: a contact form, a quote request, a booking link or an email button. Include who checks the destination, how an out-of-hours request is handled and what happens if a connected service fails. If notifications rely on an individual's mailbox, decide whether that is appropriate or whether a business-owned inbox would make coverage easier.

Use dummy data for a test enquiry and tell the receiving team in advance. Check the message arrives once, to the expected destination, with the context needed to respond. Verify the form shows a meaningful confirmation and that staff can distinguish the test from a customer request. Where there are multiple service lines or locations, test a representative route for each distinct destination. One successful contact form does not prove an independent booking integration is working.

## Set access and support boundaries

Assign named accounts and give people the permissions needed for their work. Make sure the business has a documented recovery path, with a backup administrator where the platform supports it. Use your organisation's approved approach to multifactor authentication and secure credential storage. A handover note should identify who manages access, not expose the information needed to impersonate them.

Agree which agency access remains for maintenance and which should end. Make a dated list of people and integrations to review after the business has proved it can operate. Do not disable a deployment integration just because its name looks unfamiliar; identify its purpose and replace it safely if needed. Confirm who receives incident alerts and where staff should report a fault.

If the agency will continue support, distinguish defects, routine maintenance and new work. State how to report an urgent outage, where updates will arrive and what the stated support period covers. If a tool or account cannot yet transfer, record the temporary dependency, the person responsible and the next check date. A visible exception is better than promising independence while one critical login still belongs to someone else.

## Run a witnessed acceptance test

Choose practical actions, assign them to the people who will do the job and record the outcome. These checks are a starting point, not a requirement to change production settings during the meeting:

- The business can locate its domain, see renewal details and identify where DNS is managed.
- A developer can clone the repository, build the site and deploy a harmless change to preview.
- An editor can update and undo a representative content change.
- A test enquiry reaches the expected system; staff can locate it and see its context.
- A named owner can open the correct analytics and Search Console properties with their own account.
- The operator can explain which backup or version would be restored for a broken release or lost content.
- The person managing the handover can identify billing contacts, upcoming renewals and known exceptions.

An illustrative example: a service business receives a repository link and successfully publishes a preview, but the new team cannot edit an enquiry routing rule. The outgoing agency still controls that provider account. Mark deployment as passed and routing control as open. Assign a named owner to arrange the appropriate access or replacement, then repeat the dummy enquiry. Do not label the overall handover complete just because the code was delivered.

Leave the team with the inventory, short runbooks, dates and the evidence from these checks. Store the handover record where the business can find it even after a project workspace closes. Put the next renewal and the first access review on an internal calendar. Future hires should be able to identify the right account and responsible colleague without starting the investigation all over again.

## Common handover questions

### Is a ZIP file enough?

It can be part of a simple handover, but it does not demonstrate that you can recreate the live site or maintain its connected services. Ask how to rebuild the files, where editable content and records live, and who has permission to publish. The right deliverables depend on the platform and the agreement.

### Should we change hosts during the handover?

Not automatically. First decide what problem a host change would solve. Keeping infrastructure stable can make it easier to isolate ownership and access issues. If a move is necessary, plan it as a separate change with checks for DNS, email, hosting, redirects and recovery. Document the order and the people responsible.

### What should we ask for before signing a new website project?

Agree which assets and accounts the business will control, what will be delivered at the end and who will lead the acceptance session. The [website redesign brief guide](/blog/website-redesign-brief-before-hiring-an-agency) helps you capture those expectations while scope and ownership are still being discussed.

## Plan a handover your team can actually use

Start with the accounts that would stop the business from operating if one familiar person were unavailable. Then test a small set of actions that puts those assumptions to work. The aim is not to collect the largest possible bundle of documentation. It is to know that someone at the business can make the next change, respond to the next enquiry and recover if something goes wrong.

Do not include passwords or private keys in the enquiry.
